title: Iran's Oil Minister Resigns as Aramco Warns Inventories Are 'Scarily Thin'
subhead: Tehran hands its most important industry to a sanctioned NIOC chief as oil revenues approach zero, while Saudi Aramco's CEO says the world has burned through roughly 1 billion barrels of spare stock and could take up to two years to refill.

sections.heading: Iran Replaces Its Oil Minister With the Man Already Under U.S. Sanctions
sections.body:
Iran's oil minister, Mohsen Paknejad, resigned and President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted the departure on Sunday, appointing Hamid Bovard — the head of the National Iranian Oil Company — as acting oil minister, Reuters reported. The president's office framed the resignation as long-requested and personal, but the timing is the story: Washington is actively trying to cut Iran's remaining exports to zero.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Saturday that Iran had no oil shipments left at sea and would generate zero oil revenue this week, according to Anadolu Agency. Iran's central bank governor had already said in August that oil exports had effectively fallen to zero. The rial hit a record low of about 2.688 million to the dollar last week and inflation has climbed above 70%, per Reuters.

Bovard, 62, is already sanctioned — the U.S. Treasury designated him in February 2025 for operating in Iran's petroleum sector and its so-called shadow fleet. He has run NIOC since 2024 and spent most of his career in oilfield operations. His appointment puts a technocrat with no diplomatic profile in charge of an industry whose problem is now access to buyers and shipping, not production capability.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran is separating the political face of its oil sector from its sanctions-exposed operating core. Naming an already-sanctioned insider signals Tehran expects no near-term relief and is optimizing for moving barrels covertly, not for negotiating exports back into the open market.

sections.heading: Aramco's CEO: The System Has Already Burned Through Its Cushion
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday that the world has lost nearly 3 billion barrels of gross oil supply since the Iran war began — roughly half the crude and products that would normally have moved through the Strait of Hormuz over the same period. He said more than 1 billion barrels have been drawn from inventories, mostly onshore commercial stocks, leaving under 6 billion barrels in commercial inventory, the vast majority of which he described as not practically available.

'The system is already straining,' Nasser said, adding that the supply resilience cushion is 'scarily thin.' He told the forum that Brent could have reached $200 per barrel without Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which lets Riyadh bypass Hormuz by moving crude to the Red Sea — Bloomberg and The National both carried the remarks. Flows on that line have been restored to about 80% of capacity following an attack last month.

Nasser said refilling inventories while still meeting demand could take as long as two years even after Hormuz fully reopens, and warned that emergency reserves 'might buy us a winter' but cannot fix long-term supply. Aramco, he added, is studying additional export routes and overseas storage, and can make its full 12 million bpd of sustainable capacity available within days.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the clearest public number yet on how much of the world's buffer has been consumed. It reframes the recent Hormuz flow recovery: crude is moving again, but the inventory cushion that absorbed the shock is now thin enough that a single fresh disruption — a refinery hit, a pipeline attack — has far less slack to fall back on.

sections.heading: Aramco Splits Its Pricing: Deep Cut for Asia, a Hike for Europe
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco cut November prices for Asian buyers to their lowest in six years while raising prices for European-bound cargoes by $3 per barrel, Reuters reported, citing company pricing. Arab Light will sell at a $5 per barrel discount to the Dubai/Oman benchmark for Asia — a $3 cut and the lowest since June 2020. Prices for U.S. buyers were left unchanged. Analysts had expected hikes.

The Asian discount reads as a response to freight economics, not softening demand. Because Riyadh is using ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman to move crude past Hormuz with less exposure to Iranian attack — smaller vessels carry oil out, then offload onto VLCCs waiting off Oman — shipping costs have exploded. Poten & Partners data cited by Gulf News shows VLCC freight at an all-time high of $1.3 million per day, up roughly 43-fold from about $30,000 per day in January. Freight now adds about $33 per barrel to Persian Gulf cargoes, versus $1.73 in January — 27% of delivered cost, up from 3%.
sections.whyItMatters: Aramco is effectively absorbing freight pain to keep Asian market share while charging Europe, which has fewer alternatives, full price. The pricing gap is a live measure of how much value the market now assigns to the Hormuz risk premium — and how differently Asia and Europe are treated on it.

sections.heading: Hormuz Crude Flows Edge Above Pre-War Levels — LNG Does Not
sections.body:
Kpler provisional data, reported by Reuters, shows crude flows out of Hormuz ranged between 19.5 and 22.5 million barrels daily from September 27 to 29 — roughly double the level of a month earlier and above pre-war levels. Brent traded around $101 and WTI around $90 on Monday, barely moving, which traders read as skepticism that the improvement is durable.

The LNG picture is far worse. LNG traffic through Hormuz remains more than 75% below pre-war levels despite at least three carriers transiting outbound since late last week, per Bloomberg and Kpler data. Only 21 LNG cargoes are estimated to have exited the strait in September — the highest monthly count since the war began, but a fraction of the pre-war norm of roughly three cargoes per day. Most carriers are now running dark mode, AIS off, which makes flows harder to count. QatarEnergy remains in force majeure on exports even as it reportedly looks to buy cargoes to service long-term contracts.

The strait also remains unsafe. UK Maritime Trade Operations reported an attack on a tanker on Sunday — the eighth vessel hit by an unknown projectile in the past week.
sections.whyItMatters: Crude and gas are diverging: tankers have found a workaround for oil via ship-to-ship transfers, but LNG — which needs specialized ships and terminals — has no equivalent fix. Gas buyers in Asia and Europe are still competing for non-Hormuz supply, which is why the recovery in headline oil volumes has not translated into relief on the gas side.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Holds November Quota at 31.01 Million bpd — and Keeps Producing Below It
sections.body:
OPEC+ agreed on Sunday to keep its November quota unchanged at 31.01 million barrels per day for the eight members covered, in line with expectations, per OPEC. But the group produced only about 25 million bpd in August, well below its own ceiling — meaning most of the production-cut unwind announced earlier this year exists largely on paper while Hormuz was paralyzed.

UBS commodity analyst Giovanni Staunovo, quoted by Reuters, noted that output remains below quota despite rising Hormuz flows, so 'the oil market remains tight.' The puzzle — more oil moving through Hormuz without more oil being produced — is only partly explained by storage releases; Kpler data cited by Reuters put the Middle East seven-day moving average at 18.5 million bpd in the week to October 1 (Hormuz, Gulf of Oman and Bab el-Mandeb combined).
sections.whyItMatters: OPEC+ is holding a quota it cannot hit, which means the cartel's headline numbers no longer describe physical supply. With spare capacity already thin, the gap between the paper ceiling and real output tells traders that OPEC+ has limited room to add barrels if the next disruption hits.

sections.heading: Asia Rewires Its Supply Map: Korea Triples Canadian Crude, Signs $8.4bn U.S. EOR Deal
sections.body:
The share of Saudi crude in South Korea's imports fell below 30% for the first time since 2021, at 29.9% for January–August, according to Yonhap citing Korea National Oil Corp. and the Korea Petroleum Association. U.S. crude's share topped 20% for the first time in April and has stayed there. Seoul agreed with Canada in June to triple Canadian crude imports and boost Canadian LNG purchases, and aims to cut Middle East crude reliance to 50% by 2035.

Separately, President Donald Trump said Friday that South Korea's U.S. investment agreement includes $8.4 billion for an enhanced oil recovery project — a claim Seoul's industry ministry denied, saying no such item was in the strategic investment agreement and that it has asked Washington for clarification, per Yonhap. Trump also cited a $200 billion Korean commitment to U.S. projects including eight large nuclear plants, a 6-GW Texas power facility and a pipeline tied to Alaska LNG; Seoul says Alaska participation remains subject to commercial viability and legal review with no FID yet.
sections.whyItMatters: The world's most import-dependent economies are not waiting for Hormuz to normalize — they are locking in non-Gulf barrels and tying energy investment to security guarantees. The U.S.-Korea gap over the EOR figure shows how much of that reshuffling is being announced for political effect before the commercial terms exist.

sections.heading: Yemen Re-escalates as a Saudi Refinery Fire Tests the Kingdom's Infrastructure
sections.body:
Reports of a possible attack on Saudi Arabia's Petro Rabigh refining and petrochemical complex north of Jeddah circulated Monday. Iran's Tasnim news agency, citing Yemeni sources, reported a refinery attack near Jeddah, but Saudi authorities and Aramco have not confirmed one, per Oilprice and Newsquawk. Video circulating on Telegram and satellite thermal readings appeared consistent with a fire at or near storage infrastructure, though the footage's authenticity and timing were not independently verified. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline was reported by Bloomberg to be operating normally after earlier reports claimed an attack had halted it.

The context is a sharp re-escalation in Yemen: the internationally recognized government announced a major military campaign to retake Houthi-held territory, per Al Jazeera. The last time Rabigh came under fire was in March 2022, during a wave of drone and missile strikes on Saudi energy assets including Yanbu LNG facilities. Oil prices barely reacted — WTI at $90.74 and Brent at $102.16, both roughly flat.
sections.whyItMatters: With Aramco's inventory cushion thin, the market's muted reaction to a possible refinery hit is itself notable — traders appear to be discounting single-facility damage. But renewed Houthi activity against Saudi energy infrastructure is exactly the kind of event that tests the newly restored Hormuz flow, and the denial-versus-claim gap means the physical picture is still unresolved.

bottomLine: Iran's oil ministry changed hands Sunday, with a sanctions-designated NIOC insider now running an industry whose export revenue Washington says has hit zero — a signal Tehran is preparing for prolonged covert selling rather than near-term relief. The bigger numbers came from Aramco: Nasser says the war has consumed roughly 1 billion barrels of the world's inventory buffer, leaving under 6 billion barrels of commercial stock and a refill timeline of up to two years. Crude flows through Hormuz have recovered to pre-war levels, but LNG remains down more than 75% and OPEC+ is producing well below its own quota, so the physical market is tighter than the headline recovery suggests — and the cushion that absorbed this shock is far thinner going into winter.
sources: Oilprice.com, Reuters, Bloomberg, Anadolu Agency, The National, Yonhap/Korea Times, OPEC, U.S. Treasury, IEA, Kpler, UKMTO, Poten & Partners, Gulf News, UBS, Al Jazeera, Tasnim, Newsquawk
